qt: to the Commission Ioan-Rareş Bogdan (PPE) Subject:

The way in which Europeans access information has changed rapidly in recent years, with the increasing use of digital tools and artificial intelligence.1 In 2025, 32.7 % of EU citizens aged between 16 and 74 had used AI tools. Meanwhile, the consumption of e-books and audiobooks has grown, showing a transformation in the way Europeans access written content. The development of AI provides fast access to information and can be an aid to learning but the frequent use of tools that provide instant information and responses can influence the way in which people, especially young people, approach long texts and in-depth reading. 1.

Is the Commission considering monitoring the effects of using artificial intelligence on the reading habits of Europeans, especially children and young people, and assessing its impact on in-depth reading, the ability to concentrate and text comprehension?
What steps is the Commission taking to encourage reading and the development of lasting relationships with books in an environment where instant access to information is becoming ever more present?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.10.2026) According to the Programme for International Student Assessment 20251, one-in-three 15year-olds in the EU frequently use AI to summarise text. While evidence on the impact on reading comprehension remains limited, research shows that the effect on learning outcomes depend on the nature and the use of AI. To promote a critical engagement with AI, the Commission and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development presented an AI literacy framework2. The Guidelines on the ethical use of AI and data3 in teaching and learning and the Guidelines for teachers on promoting digital literacy and tackling disinformation4, support teachers in making informed choices about AI and in raising awareness about disinformation. To address the decline in literacy competences and reading and deliver on the Action Plan on Basic Skills5, the Commission is establishing the European Literacy Coalition. It also promotes reading through the European Authors Day initiative, encouraging young people to discover European literature and highlighting the EU’s linguistic and cultural diversity. Through Creative Europe, the Commission supports projects strengthening the circulation of European literary works, promoting translation, fostering audience development, and reinforcing sectoral competitiveness and resilience. The Apply AI Strategy boosts trustworthy innovative adoption of AI in key sectors, including in education. The forthcoming Education Package will support further basic skills, teachers and human-centred AI. Member States make use of EU structural funding, including the European Regional Development Fund, supporting the construction, renovation and modernisation of libraries. These play a key role in promoting literacy, social inclusion, and democratic participation. The report on the role of public libraries6 also highlights their importance.
